data.title: X rolls out parental controls for teens, but parents face a limitation
data.description:
Social media platform X has introduced parental controls for teenage accounts, allowing parents and guardians to monitor screen time, approve new followers and restrict content recommendations. However, the new features come with a limitation that teenagers must agree to link their accounts with those of their parents before supervision can begin.
 
The announcement, made by X's official Safety account, marks the platform's introduction of dedicated parental supervision tools. The features are designed for users aged 13 to 17 and give parents some control over their children's activity without granting them access to private conversations or browsing histories.

How will X's parental controls work?

Parents and guardians can link their accounts with those of their teenagers through an invitation. The teenager must accept the request before the parental controls can be activated. The invitation remains valid for 72 hours.
 
 
Once the accounts are linked, parents can view how much time their teenager has spent on X over the previous seven days and set daily screen-time limits. They can also restrict access to certain features and manage aspects of their children's interactions on the platform.
 
X allows parents to require approval before new accounts can follow their teenagers. Enabling this option also makes the teenager's account private.
 
Parents can additionally restrict recommendations and videos in the For You feed to accounts their teenagers already follow. They can filter content by blocking specific words and switch off the display of sensitive media. ALSO READ: WhatsApp partners with Jio, Verizon, more to bring travel eSIM data plans

Parents can restrict DMs, but cannot read private messages

The new controls allow parents to decide who can send direct messages to their teenagers. They can also see which accounts their children have exchanged one-to-one messages with.
 
However, parents will not be able to read the actual conversations. They will also not have access to their teenagers' search or viewing histories, or be able to post on their behalf or take control of their accounts. 
ALSO READ: Apple removes Chinese AI chatbot from App Store over child safety concerns

Teenagers can refuse parental supervision

One of the key limitations of the new feature is that parents cannot activate supervision without their teenagers' consent.
 
The teenager must accept the invitation sent by the parent before the accounts can be linked. This gives teenagers the option to decline parental supervision, even if their parents want to enable the controls.
 
A parent can supervise up to five teenage accounts, while each teenager can be linked to only one parent or guardian.

What happens when teenagers turn 18?

The parental supervision arrangement is intended for users aged 13 to 17. The supervision link automatically ends when the teenager turns 18.

data.title: ADB signs $75 million loan with Veritas Finance to expand MSME lending
data.description:
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has signed a $75 million loan agreement with Veritas Finance Ltd (VFL) to expand lending to micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in India, with at least 30 per cent of the financing earmarked for eligible women borrowers.
 
The financing forms part of ADB's project to expand access to finance for MSMEs through Veritas Finance.
 
The ADB-supported transaction has also mobilised $55 million in parallel loans from commercial lenders and includes technical assistance to help VFL develop a dedicated secured term-loan product for women borrowers.
 
The project is aimed at helping narrow India's MSME financing gap, estimated at more than $300 billion, while expanding access to formal credit for small businesses, including women-owned enterprises.
  
The transaction marks Veritas Finance's first external commercial borrowing and its first syndicated US dollar loan.
 
It is also expected to help the India-based lender diversify its funding sources and establish a presence in the international loan market, potentially paving the way for future offshore fund-raising.
 
“Many small businesses in rural and semi-urban areas in India struggle to get the credit they need to grow,” said Mio Oka, ADB country director for India.
 
“ADB is helping Veritas raise long-term funding from international lenders and develop a business loan tailored to women borrowers. This will help Veritas reach more small businesses that have difficulty getting a bank loan,” she added.
 
D Arulmany, chief executive officer of Veritas Finance, said the partnership marked an important milestone in the company's next phase of growth.
 
“By combining ADB’s institutional strength with Veritas team's innovation and execution, we are well-positioned to further scale our impact by addressing critical development needs of the vastly underbanked semi-urban and rural businesses, particularly women entrepreneurs,” he said.
 
Veritas Finance is a non-banking financial company registered with the Reserve Bank of India.
 
The company began operations in 2015 with a focus on the financial needs of semi-urban and rural markets.
 
It offers secured business loans, used commercial vehicle loans, affordable housing loans and working-capital finance.
 
As of September 2026, Veritas Finance had a loan portfolio of about $1.1 billion and operated across more than 500 locations in 10 states.

data.title: Tamil Nadu's share of Lok Sabha seats must remain intact: MK Stalin
data.description:
Former Tamil Nadu chief minister and Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DKM) supremo MK Stalin on Friday maintained that the state’s existing 7.18 per cent share of Lok Sabha seats must not be reduced under any circumstances if the number of parliamentary constituencies is increased through delimitation. He also demanded that the existing proportion of parliamentary representation among states, based on the 1971 Census, remain unchanged for another 25 years.
 
His comments came ahead of a special sitting of Parliament, which the government has convened from November 30 to December 3 to transact “essential government business”.
 
In a post on X, Stalin said the DMK would not compromise on the two demands, which were part of resolutions passed by the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly and the Joint Action Committee on fair delimitation.
 
 
“If the number of parliamentary constituencies is increased, under no circumstances should Tamil Nadu’s existing 7.18 per cent share of seats in the lower house be reduced,” Stalin said.
 
He added that the existing proportion of parliamentary representation among states, determined on the basis of the 1971 Census and frozen earlier, must remain unchanged for another 25 years.
 
“The DMK stands firm on these two demands and will continue to do so. There is no change in our position, and there is no question of any compromise,” he said.
 
Stalin also said the DMK was the first party in the country to raise concerns about the possible consequences of delimitation. He said Chennai hosted the first meeting that brought together national political leaders to demand a fair delimitation exercise.

Centre plans special Parliament sitting

The Lok Sabha will reconvene on November 30, while the Rajya Sabha will meet on December 2. The sittings will conclude on December 3, subject to the requirements of government business, according to official sources.
 
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced the decision on X on Thursday. The special sitting will be an extension of the Monsoon Session, which was adjourned sine die on August 13 but was not formally prorogued.
 
The Union Cabinet is also expected to discuss the delimitation-linked women's reservation proposal ahead of the special sitting, news agency PTI reported.
 
The development has renewed speculation about the government's plans to reintroduce the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which was defeated in Parliament in April.

What does the proposed Delimitation Bill seek to change?

The proposed Constitution amendment seeks to increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from the existing 550 to 850 members. This would include up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union Territories, according to the provisions outlined in the proposed legislation.
 
The Bill also seeks to change the framework governing the allocation of parliamentary seats among states and Union Territories, allowing Parliament to determine which Census figures will be used for delimitation.
 
The separate Delimitation Bill, 2026, provides for the constitution of a Delimitation Commission to readjust and reallocate seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies.
 
It proposes using the latest published Census figures available when the commission is constituted. This could mean that the next delimitation exercise will use the 2011 Census, the latest published Census data currently available.
 
The proposed constitutional amendment also seeks to bring forward the implementation of 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies.
 
Under the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, women's reservation was linked to the completion of a Census followed by delimitation. The proposed amendment seeks to remove the requirement of waiting for a fresh Census and enable the quota to take effect following delimitation based on the latest published Census figures.
 
The government aims to implement the reservation ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.

Previous attempt to pass the Bill failed

The government had introduced the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, alongside the Delimitation Bill, 2026, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill during a special sitting of Parliament in April.
 
However, the Constitution amendment failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha on April 17. Of the 528 members who voted, 298 supported the Bill and 230 opposed it. The proposal fell short of the required 352 votes.
 
The defeat rendered the two related Bills infructuous, and they were not taken up for consideration.

data.title: Over 500 cops deployed for Diljit's Mumbai concert after bomb threat
data.description:
More than 500 Mumbai police personnel will be deployed at Mahalaxmi Racecourse here for actor-singer Diljit Dosanjh's concert on Friday following a threat email warning of possible attacks on the venue and Metro stations, officials said.

Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad (BDDS) teams have swept the venue, they said, adding that entry checks will be carried out across all five gates instead of three.

Private security personnel have also been roped in to assist police, an official said.

An email threatening blasts, grenade attacks and planting of IEDs at the mayor's office, metro rail stations and Dosanjh's concert was received on Thursday, the anniversary of the devastating 26/11 terror attacks.

 

The email, sent by an individual identifying herself as Hannah Meler, contained references to Khalistan, the 1984 anti-Sikh riots as well as threats of violence linked to a programme involving Dosanjh and people associated with the event.

In view of the threat, the Mumbai police has deployed around 200 constables, 150 women constables and 75 officers, besides plainclothes personnel stationed around the singer. Dog squads and an Anti-Narcotics Cell (ANC) team will also remain present at the venue, an official said.

He said that a no-car zone extending 500 to 700 metres around the racecourse will be enforced, and parking will not be permitted at the event, though no road diversions have been announced.

Organisers have been instructed not to disclose details of the singer's hotel or arrival time as part of the security protocol, sources said.

Meanwhile, organisers have prohibited posters, banners, signs and flags of any kind inside Mahalaxmi Racecourse for the concert, which is part of Dosanjh's RuPay AURA India Tour 2026.

data.title: Glenmark Pharma hits new high, up 5th straight day; gains 35% from Oct low
data.description:
Glenmark Pharmaceuticals share price movement

 
Glenmark Pharmaceuticals’ share price hit a new high of ₹2,846, rallying 4 per cent on the BSE in Friday’s intraday deals in an otherwise weak market due to better business outlook. In comparison, the BSE Sensex was down 0.84 per cent at 83,624 at 01:07 PM.
 
The stock price of the pharma company quoted higher for the fifth straight day, surging 9 per cent. It bounced back 35 per cent from its previous month low of ₹2,103 touched on October 23, 2026.
 

Glenmark Pharma – Q2 results

 
On a like-for-like basis, Glenmark Pharma said consolidated revenue grew approximately 20 per cent year-on-year (YoY). Its India formulations business recorded revenue of ₹1,327 crore, growing 14 per cent, while North America revenue stood at ₹1,209 crore. Excluding deferred out-licensing income recognition for ISB 2001, the core North American business grew approximately 31 per cent. Europe revenue increased 6.2 per cent to ₹792 crore, while emerging markets revenue grew 33.2 per cent to ₹877 crore.
 
 
Glenn Saldanha, chairman and managing director of Glenmark Pharmaceuticals, said the company remained on track to deliver its FY27 guidance, supported by continued growth in India, a recovery in North America and robust performance in emerging markets.
 
The company expects the first launch from its partnered innovative oncology pipeline by the end of FY27. Its innovation arm, Ichnos Glenmark Innovation, is also advancing its multispecific oncology pipeline, with Phase I data for ISB 2001 selected for an oral presentation at the 2026 American Society of Hematology Annual Meeting.
 
Glenmark's India formulation business recorded a growth of 16.7 per cent in the second quarter and 15.7 per cent as per moving annual total (MAT) September 2026 data, compared to the Indian Pharmaceutical Market (IPM) growth of 13.8 per cent in Q2 and 12.1 per cent in MAT September. Glenmark continues to sustain strong growth in its core therapeutic areas like dermatology, respiratory, cardiac, and oncology.
 
As the operating leverage kicks in H2FY27, the management expects gross debt to be zero by end of FY27. The company remains focused on the prudent capital allocation, and accordingly, the management said the company is focusing on its strategic growth targets and maintaining healthy balance sheet ratios. 
 

Motilal Oswal Financial Services view on Glenmark Pharma

 
Glenmark Pharma delivered a better-than-expected operational performance in Q2FY27, with a 5 per cent beat on revenue/ earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA). Earnings were largely in line as the impact of higher-than-expected EBITDA was offset by lower other income, analysts at Motilal Oswal Financial Services said.
 
On a like-to-like basis, Glenmark Pharma outperformed the industry in the domestic formulation segment by almost 300bp for the quarter, backed by superior execution in cardiology, dermatology and respiratory segments. It continued to launch differentiated oncology, respiratory as well as dermatology products, supporting better growth prospects in the domestic formulation (DF) segment, the brokerage firm said.
 
The strategic reset in DF and new launches in North America has led to improved performance and a better outlook going forward. The clinical development related to innovative oncology and immunology molecules is progressing on track. Also, the company intends to be gross debt zero by FY27, strengthening the balance sheet, the brokerage firm said, as it maintains a 'Buy' rating on the stock with a target price of ₹3,000 per share. Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion.

data.title: 43 WTC wickets, 21.28 avg since Oval: Why is Siraj out of India's XI?
data.description:
When Jasprit Bumrah handed India's Test cap No. 321 to Gurnoor Brar at Hagley Oval on Friday morning, the moment captured the defining tension of the Gautam Gambhir coaching era. Out in the middle, a tall, raw fast bowler was being rewarded for a breakout white-ball tour with a dream red-ball debut on one of world cricket's premier seam-bowling decks. Beyond the boundary rope, wearing dark sunglasses as broadcast cameras lingered on him, stood Mohammed Siraj—India's leading wicket-taker in the 2025-27 World Test Championship, benched for a second consecutive overseas Test to end a six-year streak of playing in every away series since his 2020 debut.
 
 
Beside Siraj in the dugout sat Ravindra Jadeja, similarly overlooked for both Wellington and Christchurch. Thousands of kilometres away in Mumbai, wrist-spinner Kuldeep Yadav—originally named in the New Zealand Test squad—was bowling four-over spells for Uttar Pradesh against Mizoram in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy, having been released from the tour nearly two weeks earlier.
 
Across India's New Zealand assignment, Gambhir and captain Shubman Gill have pursued an unmistakably unsentimental blueprint: prioritize current rhythm over reputation, stretch batting depth deep into the lower order, and hand emerging fast bowlers real Test exposure in pace-friendly conditions. The result has ignited one of the sharpest selection debates in recent Indian cricket, pitting the long-term promise of a new pace crop against the jarring sight of proven match-winners being shown the exit.
 
The Siraj Data: What the numbers actually say
 
Nothing illustrates the debate better than the stark statistical split in Mohammed Siraj's career before and after his defining nine-wicket performance (4/86 and 5/104) at The Oval in August 2025, which sealed a six-run victory and a 2-2 series draw in England.
 
On the surface, dropping Siraj looks baffling. Far from declining after London, his overall output actually surged. Across the seven Tests following The Oval, Siraj claimed 21 wickets at an average of 21.28 and a strike rate of 44.3—a dramatic improvement on the seven Tests immediately preceding it (three in Australia, four in England), where he averaged 40.04 and struck every 58.4 balls. Even in home conditions, where pacers traditionally toil, his average dropped from 37.00 before The Oval (19 wickets in 14 Tests) to 20.23 afterward (17 wickets in five).

Dig deeper into the post-Oval window, however, and the reason behind the management's unease emerges. Siraj's seven Tests since London divide cleanly into two halves:
 
  • The 2025 peak: In four home Tests against the West Indies and South Africa between October and November 2025, Siraj was lethal—taking 16 wickets at 19.00 (SR 36.8), highlighted by 7/71 in Ahmedabad and 4/49 in Kolkata.
  • The 2026 stall: Across three Asian Tests in 2026—against Afghanistan in New Chandigarh and two Tests in Sri Lanka—his penetration dried up. He managed just five wickets at 28.60, needing 68.4 deliveries per breakthrough. In Sri Lanka specifically, he conceded just 2.34 runs an over across 44 overs, but took exactly one wicket in each of four innings (4 wickets, SR 66.0).
 
Crucially, his bowling volume had also contracted sharply—36.3% fewer deliveries across the seven post-Oval Tests (930 balls vs. 1,460 before), dropping from 34.8 overs per match to 22.1. After conceding 140 runs in 25 overs for South Zone in the Duleep Trophy final, Siraj diagnosed the issue not as fatigue from his 305.3-over workload under Gill, but as rust caused by long gaps between Tests. "I'm purely a rhythm bowler. If I'm not in sync, I simply can't explode through the crease. That was the struggle in Sri Lanka, my run-up felt disjointed," he admitted.
 
Yet even that explanation leaves the management's verdict open to scrutiny. At Hagley Oval itself in early November, Siraj looked back in sync, claiming 4/118 in 35 overs for India A against New Zealand A. Instead of getting another red-ball outing, he was flown to Mount Maunganui for the final ODI—where he dismissed Tim Seifert and Finn Allen—only to be told he was not at his "peak" when the Tests began. 
Cricket experts' push back: 'Where was Mohammed Siraj?'
 
That narrow 2026 subcontinental sample was nowhere near enough to convince former players and analysts that India should sideline a proven overseas workhorse in New Zealand—and the backlash only sharpened after the toss at Hagley Oval on Friday confirmed Siraj had been overlooked for a second consecutive Test.
 
Even from the opposition camp, the surprise was unmistakable. Speaking after the Christchurch toss, former New Zealand fast bowler Chris Martin admitted the hosts were relieved not to face him on a green seamers' track: "We are probably happy, from a New Zealand perspective, that Siraj is not playing, as he would've loved this pitch."
 
Earlier in the series, former India head coach Ravi Shastri had cut straight to the contradiction on X after Wellington: "If pace, skill and seam movement were the criteria, and 140 clicks was hard to come by, one has to ask the question. Where was MOHD SIRAJ? Experience, aggression and the ability to make things happen with the ball. Surely that counts for something!" Dinesh Karthik, speaking on Cricbuzz, likewise noted that Siraj's 2026 dip came entirely on flat subcontinental tracks: "He's shown that he's someone who can bowl really long spells. He can also bowl for 20-22 overs in a day. He's a workhorse and an absolute champion when it comes to the attitude that's required in Test matches." 
Mohammed Siraj stats. Source: Cricinfo
 
Once Gurnoor Brar was handed his debut cap ahead of Siraj in Christchurch, the post-toss criticism escalated across broadcast panels and social media:
  • Harsha Bhogle (on X) warned of the psychological message sent to India's pace group: "Siraj is now India's 6th ranked fast bowler. I find it so unfair. Of the top 5 wicket takers in test cricket in this WTC cycle, India now have place only for Bumrah. You wish the bowlers selected well, they have great conditions to bowl in, but they will know they won't get a long rope when it is their turn."
  • Ravichandran Ashwin, who had called the Wellington double omission of Siraj and Ravindra Jadeja "very harsh" and the "new normal," doubled down with pointed sarcasm on X during Day 1 in Christchurch. "While Akash Deep has been unplayable today, Siraj clearly looks like he has lost his bowling mojo. Hope he trains hard & tries to get back in time for the BGT," Ashwin wrote—before adding as New Zealand's middle order steadied late in the day: "This 60-80 over mark is usually the easiest time to bat & I hope Siraj can run in hard and get a breakthrough or two."
  • Mohammad Kaif (on X) questioned the mixed messaging from the camp: "Hard to believe as one of India's premier fast bowler Mohammed Siraj is dropped again. Siraj should be one of the first names considered in India's overseas Test bowling attack, alongside Bumrah. Interestingly, bowling coach Morne Morkel himself called Siraj a world-class bowler and said he was bowling well."
  • Murali Kartik (on Sony Sports) was visibly frustrated after broadcast cameras showed an emotional-looking Siraj walking near the boundary in sunglasses post-toss. "With the numbers you've seen so far, I am surprised. For what reason? Either don't keep him in the team at all then," Kartik fumed alongside Ajinkya Rahane. "If you feel his form isn't good, or he's not bowling well in the nets, or wherever, I don't know whatever the thinking might be, then don't take him on the tour at all. Don't take him; what's the point then?"
  • Sunil Gavaskar (on Sony Sports) broadened the post-toss critique to include Jadeja while ultimately choosing to rally behind the selected XI. "Well, we are only talking about Siraj, but what about Jadeja? He is India's third-highest wicket-taker in this WTC cycle. I do believe his spin would've been pretty useful on the fourth and fifth days... So, tough luck for him as well as Mohammed Siraj," Gavaskar said. "Now, Siraj is among the top wicket-takers in the cycle. So, let's wait and see. The way I've always seen it is that whatever reservations you might have about the XI, the 14 or the 16, once the team is selected, it is your team and my team. It's an Indian team. So, I back this team now that they've picked this playing XI, and I'm praying that this team does well."
 
The 'bowlers who can bat' doctrine and the Kuldeep Paradox
 
 Siraj's omission cannot be viewed in isolation. It sits inside a wider philosophical shift under Gambhir—one defined by batting depth, left-right matchups, and multi-skill utility players. Washington Sundar himself acknowledged earlier this year that Gambhir prefers packing the XI with all-rounders who can plug multiple roles.
 
In New Zealand, that philosophy reshaped both the spin and pace departments. Rather than pick pure strike bowlers, India opted for a tail that could bat: Anshul Kamboj (who struck a brisk 38 off 42 balls in India's massive 720/9 declared at Wellington), Akash Deep (13 off 5), and Washington Sundar (24 off 26) all helped extend the lower order.
 
The collateral damage was twofold. First, Ravindra Jadeja was left out for Sundar—a call that backfired on Day 5 in Wellington when New Zealand calmly batted out 120 overs for 239/5 to save the Test, with Sundar managing just 1/110 across 55 overs in the match. Former batter Subramaniam Badrinath summed up the flaw in prioritizing insurance over wicket-taking penetration: "Sundar didn't do anything wrong, but you have to win the Test match. Jadeja could have been the difference. Though you got 720 runs, you couldn't finish off the match. On Day 5, Jadeja could have easily been effective."
 
Second—and perhaps most tellingly—was the BCCI's November 14 decision to release Kuldeep Yadav from the Test squad to play domestic cricket back home while drafting in Gurnoor Brar. Kuldeep boasts a Test bowling average of 23.36 and a strike rate of 39.38 across 19 matches, yet averages 12.60 with the bat.
 
New Zealand leg-spinner Ish Sodhi, speaking to PTI ahead of the Christchurch Test, laid bare the brutal math working against specialist wrist-spinners in Gambhir's setup: "Kuldeep is competing in those conditions with guys like Washington Sundar and Ravindra Jadeja, who both average 40 with the bat, if not more, in Test cricket. I can understand it from a selection point of view. From an emotional point of view, it sucks."
 
Former India captain Sourav Ganguly was far less forgiving after India failed to bowl New Zealand out in Wellington, taking to X to challenge the blurring of roles: "Washington can play as an allrounder ..@bcci where is Kuldeep or Manav Suthar?"
 
The counter-argument: Why Gambhir's youth gamble matters
 
For all the legitimate criticism of how senior match-winners have been handled, dismissing Gambhir's New Zealand strategy as mere T20-style tinkering misses an equally important reality: Indian Test cricket has historically struggled to blood young fast bowlers in forgiving seam conditions before they are thrown into the cauldron of Australia or England.
 
Gambhir has repeatedly championed the value of bowling attacks developed on sporting pitches—posting "Bowlers win you series!" after India's young pace unit engineered a historic ODI series triumph in New Zealand earlier this month. Carrying that conviction into the Test series meant trusting Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj, Prasidh Krishna, and Gurnoor Brar on tracks where pace actually has a voice. At Hagley Oval, fast bowlers had accounted for 444 of 484 Test wickets (91.7%) across 15 Tests heading into Friday.
 
And the young quicks have offered genuine glimpses of why the management is investing in them:
 
  • Akash Deep was India's most disciplined seamer in Wellington (3/53 in the first innings) and carried that control into Christchurch, taking two wickets on Day 1 by dismissing Tom Latham (59) and Rachin Ravindra (0). 
  • Gurnoor Brar, rewarded for his ODI Player of the Series form and praised by teammates for his character, generated steep bounce on debut at Hagley Oval and claimed Devon Conway (31) on the stroke of lunch for his maiden Test wicket. 
  • Anshul Kamboj, though inconsistent with the new ball in Christchurch, chipped in with Henry Nicholls' wicket (16) on Day 1, building on his two wickets and vital lower-order runs in Wellington. 
  • Prasidh Krishna, despite enduring a tough first innings in Wellington (1/100), bounced back with 2/23 in the second innings before making way for Brar's fresh legs on a three-day turnaround.
 
Even with Jasprit Bumrah going wicketless on Day 1 in Christchurch and Washington Sundar removing Daryl Mitchell, India's restructured attack kept New Zealand in check through a strong middle session before Tom Blundell (53*) and Glenn Phillips (36*) steered the hosts to 246/5 in 85 overs at stumps.

data.title: Only 20-30% of eligible Indian exports use FTA benefits: RBI Governor
data.description:
Only 20-30 per cent of eligible Indian exports avail tariff benefits under the country's free trade agreements (FTAs), compared with 60-70 per cent of eligible exports from partner countries to India, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra said on Friday.
 
"It is an opportunity we are leaving on the table," Malhotra said at the SME Finance & Investment Summit in Mumbai, urging micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to look beyond domestic markets and make greater use of India's expanding network of trade agreements. The RBI published his address on Friday.
 
He asked MSMEs to familiarise themselves with FTAs relevant to their products and invest in quality, standards and certification to access overseas markets.
 
 
India's expanding network of FTAs, some of which have dedicated chapters for SMEs, provides access to new markets, lower-cost quality inputs and opportunities to specialise in niche segments of global value chains, Malhotra said.
 
Labour-intensive MSME sectors, in particular, could help spread the benefits of trade more broadly, he added.
 
In a fireside chat following his address, Malhotra was asked about industry demands to extend the period for classifying a loan as a non-performing asset (NPA) from 90 days to 180 days.
 
He said the issue could instead be addressed by borrowers negotiating longer repayment tenures with banks, since the 90-day period begins only after a scheduled repayment becomes overdue.
 
"If you take the repayment period as longer, then the 90-day period will start later," he said.
 
Malhotra also called on banks to create dedicated modules at branches to guide entrepreneurs on the various schemes available to them.
 
Lending, he said, was ultimately built on trust and required relationship banking, where lenders understood businesses as well as the people behind them.
 
Banks should spend more time assessing the needs, capabilities and repayment capacity of enterprises, while borrowers should be persistent in seeking lenders' attention, he said.
 
Bank credit to MSMEs grew 27 per cent year-on-year in the 12 months ended September 2026, compared with 19.4 per cent growth in overall bank credit, Malhotra said.
 
Over the past five years, MSME credit has grown at a compound annual growth rate of around 19 per cent, with outstanding credit rising from ₹17.97 trillion in September 2021 to ₹42.89 trillion in September 2026.
 
"The credit gap has certainly not disappeared, but it has narrowed considerably, and quickly," he said.
 
The focus should now shift towards first-time borrowers, micro enterprises, women-led businesses, and units in smaller towns and rural areas, Malhotra added.
 
The RBI earlier this year raised the mandatory collateral-free loan limit for micro and small enterprises from ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh for loans sanctioned or renewed from April 1, 2026. Banks can raise the limit to ₹25 lakh for borrowers with a strong track record and financial position under their internal policies.
 
Malhotra said this was the first revision of the limit since 2010.
 
The Governor also highlighted the role of India's digital public infrastructure in improving access to finance.
 
The Account Aggregator framework facilitated loans worth around ₹3.5 trillion in FY26, he said, while the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) could potentially replicate in lending the impact that the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has had on payments.
 
However, he stressed that technology should supplement rather than replace relationship banking.
 
Malhotra outlined five priorities for MSMEs: aspiring to scale, investing in productivity, technology and innovation, exploring overseas markets, formalising operations to build lenders' confidence, and using instruments such as the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS).
 
Government support, he said, should be treated as "a catalyst, not a crutch".
 
The productivity of Indian MSMEs, measured by value added per worker, is around 26 per cent of that of large enterprises, according to Malhotra.
 
Raising productivity towards the level of top-quartile firms in advanced economies could add the equivalent of around 11 per cent of India's gross domestic product, he said.
 
He also flagged the relatively low adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) among Indian MSMEs, at around 15 per cent, compared with countries such as China, the US and Germany.
 
Addressing lenders, Malhotra said MSME lending should not be viewed merely as regulatory compliance or a target to be achieved.
 
Digital public infrastructure should strengthen, rather than replace, the personal understanding of borrowers that comes from relationship banking, he said.
 
Similarly, credit guarantees should help lenders share risk but should not become a substitute for proper due diligence.
 
Malhotra said the next phase of MSME development would depend not only on greater access to finance, but also on firms improving productivity, adopting technology, formalising their operations and using trade agreements to compete in overseas markets.

data.title: Brent to test $100 in coming days, says Mirae Asset Sharekhan; here's why
data.description:
Disclaimer: This article is written by Mohammed Imran, Research Analyst, Mirae Asset Sharekhan. Views expressed are his own. Readers' discretion is advised.
 
The optimism that saw crude oil prices hammered 20 per cent in the first half of November, after the Republican defeat in the US midterm election, is now fading. Both Brent and WTI have surged 8 per cent in the last three sessions amid escalating attacks on shipping in the Persian Gulf and Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities, which could reduce global oil supplies.
 
Brent climbed to $96.53 a barrel on Thursday afternoon, up nearly 10 per cent from $88.10 on Tuesday, as tensions increased across the Gulf. Prices held their gains after a bullish weekly EIA report showed crude and product inventories rose less than expected.
 
 

Attacks on shipping are cutting Gulf flows

The jump followed a string of attacks. Houthis struck Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's largest, along with the ports of Jeddah and Jazan. The IRGC reported that two tankers, including a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels, caught fire after hitting naval mines near Oman's Khasab port. The UK military's maritime agency also reported an explosion from an unknown projectile near a third tanker west of Dubai.
 
Independent media reports based on tanker tracking showed a 31 per cent drop in Hormuz traffic last week. Gulf oil exports, crude and refined products, averaged about 17.1 million barrels a day for the week ending November 18, according to ship-tracker Kpler, roughly 6 million short of the 23.3 million a day that flowed before the war.
 

Asian refiners under pressure amid correction in crack spread

Product markets are not following crude higher. European diesel and gasoil cracks eased but held up better than gasoline. European gasoil cracks retreated from peaks near $90 a barrel in September to around $60, while Asian gasoil fell from roughly $87 to near $53. This reflects a partial recovery in product flows and lower outright crude prices. Diesel remains well above early 2026 norms, while gasoline has largely normalised or worse. European margins turned negative for simpler configurations, with Northwest European simple refinery margins dropping into the minus $10 to $20 a barrel range as physical crude prices and freight surged. Medium and complex plants also saw sharp compression. The IEA noted that crippling crude acquisition and freight costs crushed European and Asian margins, raising the risk of economic run cuts at marginal sites.
 
Asian gasoline cracks led the drop. Singapore gasoline margins fell from a record peak above $50 a barrel in early October to around $2.67 a barrel by mid-November, the lowest since October 2023. The decline was driven by a surprise Chinese fuel export quota that boosted regional supplies, plus year-end destocking and improved Middle East product availability. Asian refiners are under the most pressure.
 

US balances provide a cushion

US crude inventories rose for a third consecutive week, adding 1.1 million barrels, supported by a 2.9-million-barrel withdrawal from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), which brings total withdrawals since March to 142 million barrels. Production edged higher to a fresh record of 14.07 mb/d, while crude exports slowed to an August low of 3.3 mb/d. Refinery demand increased by 428 kb/d to 17.34 mb/d, with the utilisation rate at its highest seasonal level in at least 30 years.
 
This elevated refinery activity helps explain the recent weakness in refined fuel prices and the continued recovery in fuel inventories, particularly gasoline. Distillate stocks, however, remain well below their five-year average, which points to lingering tightness despite the sharp decline in diesel prices. We expect in such a scenario Brent is heading to test $100 resistant in coming sessions.

data.title: Sebi looking into Tata Steel-APL Apollo deal, says minority interests key
data.description:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is looking into the proposed Tata Steel-APL Apollo transaction, with protection of minority shareholders remaining a key priority for the regulator, Sebi Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Friday.
 
“We take minority shareholders’ rights very seriously. Investor protection is very important,” Pandey told journalists on the sidelines of Assocham’s 17th Capital Markets Conference.
 
The regulator is yet to receive the revised contours of the proposed transaction after Tata Steel publicly indicated that it would re-examine the structure. Under takeover regulations, the draft offer document is ordinarily required to be filed within five working days of the public announcement. Sebi is expected to wait for the revised proposal before proceeding further.
 
 
The regulator’s comments come after institutional investors and proxy advisory firms raised concerns over the proposed transaction, prompting Tata Steel Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer T V Narendran to assure investors that the structure would be reviewed.
 
The proposed transaction involves Tata Steel acquiring a controlling stake in APL Apollo Tubes while APL Apollo acquires Tata Steel’s downstream tubes and colour-coated steel businesses.
 
Under the announced structure, Tata Steel agreed to acquire a 26.6 per cent promoter stake in APL Apollo for ₹15,510 crore and make an open offer for another 26 per cent at ₹2,301.40 per share, involving a maximum consideration of ₹16,756 crore.
 
APL Apollo, meanwhile, would acquire Tata Steel’s downstream businesses — including its tubes division, Khopoli unit and Tata Steel Colors — for ₹28,000 crore.
 
Tata Steel has already acquired around 9.91 per cent of APL Apollo through a block deal at ₹2,100 per share for approximately ₹5,825 crore.
 
The proposed transaction has faced scrutiny from institutional investors and proxy advisory firms over the valuation assigned to the businesses being transferred, the financing burden on APL Apollo and safeguards for its minority shareholders.
 
The concern centres on the simultaneous nature of the transaction: APL Apollo is expected to acquire Tata Steel’s downstream assets while Tata Steel becomes its controlling shareholder.
 
Investors have questioned whether the structure adequately protects minority shareholders as the ownership and capital structure of APL Apollo changes.
 
Pandey’s remarks indicate that Sebi is closely monitoring these issues, even as it awaits the revised transaction structure from the companies.
 
The overall transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and had earlier been targeted for completion by March 2027.

data.title: Inside the Tata Sons power struggle: The rules, the rift and the road ahead
data.description:
The battle to lead India's Tata Sons, the owner of marquee brands such as Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley Tea, headed for court on Friday after the sprawling conglomerate flouted the wishes of its controlling charity arm to reappoint ​the chairman.

Tata Trusts holds a stake of 66% in Tata Sons, but the latter's board re-appointed chairman ​N. Chandrasekaran and has decided to pursue a possible stock market listing, putting the power struggle at the centre of the standoff.

It is the ‌second such fight in a decade for one of India's oldest and most reputed business houses, after a years-long legal battle over Tata Sons' decision to remove earlier chairman Cyrus Mistry ended in the Supreme Court upholding the decision.

 

Here is how the current fight could play out, along with views of both sides and the complex structures, according to people familiar with the matter:

TRUSTS WANT CHANDRASEKARAN OUT OF KEY DECISIONS

Two of the seven charitable trusts that control Tata Sons asked the Mumbai high court on Thursday to declare Chandrasekaran's reappointment 'invalid, illegal, null and void', copies of internal memos reviewed by Reuters showed.

They also seek court directions that key decisions by Tata Sons require complete support from the charity arm.

Reuters has learnt the trusts will tell the court that the board should not have proceeded with the decision as both trust nominees did not back the chairman's reappointment.

At Friday's hearing, the trusts are expected to ask for a halt to plans for a November 30 board meeting set to decide next steps towards listing if the chief of the charity arm ‌and family head Noel Tata, as trust nominee, does not vote in favour.

The board of Tata Sons agrees to the stock market listing, ordered by the central bank, but the charity arm does not.

COURT CASE FOLLOWS BITTER PUBLIC DEBATE

Both sides have hired top lawyers to defend them and explain who can call the shots.

Lawmaker and Congress party leader Abhishek Manu Singhvi is representing the Tata Trusts led by Noel Tata.

Singhvi has previously said the dispute is about shareholder supremacy and the conglomerate cannot act like a "runaway board" independent of the controlling shareholder.

That position is disputed by Tata Group's Chandrasekaran, who has roped in Harish Salve, a former solicitor general of India who often represented the government in global forums.

In television remarks Salve has said the board's decision was in line with internal governing rules, urging the charity ​arm to get past the "I control the trusts, I control this group mindset."

WHY CAN'T THE TRUSTS CALL A SHAREHOLDER MEETING AND OUST THE CHAIRMAN?

The Tata Trusts ‌have problems of their own that weaken their influence. Formed of several affiliated charities, they could have used their voting power to call for a shareholders' meeting to effectively oust Chandrasekaran.

But a regulator has barred one of the main charities, the Sir Ratan Tata Trust, from convening its own meetings ​in a dispute over internal ‌appointments.

In turn, internal rules mean the charities currently lack the power to call for a meeting of Tata Sons shareholders.

The trusts can either wait for the deadlock to ‌lift, once the regulatory inquiry ends, or ask a court to lift the curbs, two people familiar with the matter said.

COURT FIGHT CENTRES ON 'ARTICLES OF ASSOCIATION'

At the heart of the dispute facing the court is the Tata Sons' governance framework known as the "articles of association", since Tata Trusts and Tata Sons ‌disagree on ​the interpretation of ​thee rules, which are not public.

The charity arm says Noel Tata's opposition to the reappointment was sufficient to halt the decision. It believes such decisions cannot be made in the absence of support of a majority of the trusts' two board nominees.

In this case, "majority amongst two is ‌two and not one," the charity ​arm has publicly argued.

Tata Sons' lawyer Salve disagrees, saying both trust nominees voted differently, prompting a casting vote that helped reappoint the chairman under the governance rules.
